turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I think it would be quite easy to get it back, ma'am, if you were to require it of me.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I do hope you're not suggesting I'm not worthy of marrying Jack, Mother. I'm perfectly capable of making my own decisions about my future.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I think it's high time we discussed this, Mother, and not just sat here questioning Jack's suitability.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I daresay, your prospects of securing a respectable marriage with my daughter are dwindling by the minute, young man.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Your family, sir, is not exactly one that is steeped in tradition or respectability, is it? I am not aware of any connections to the aristocracy or any illustrious titles.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, I am not impressed by your attempts to gloss over your family's dubious reputation, young man. Your own name, Worthing, is quite...unusual, is it not?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, I am astonished that you expect me to consider you a suitable husband for my daughter, given your questionable family history and dubious social standing. You will have to do better than this, Mr. Worthing, if you wish to persuade me of your worthiness.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, I find your explanation of your family's circumstances to be quite...lacking in sincerity. Your words sound more like the fabrications of a poet than the honest confessions of a respectable gentleman.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Pray, tell me, Mr. Worthing, what is this 'Bengal tiger' that you claim to have been attacked by? I should think it a most unlikely and absurd tale, and hardly a suitable anecdote for a respectable gentleman such as yourself.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, that the tiger was quite real, and I'm afraid I wasn't exaggerating when I said it was a rather fierce beast. I-I've got the scars to prove it, if you'd like to see them.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I do wish you'd stop interrogating him, Mother. He's perfectly capable of defending himself.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I would be happy to show you the scars, Lady Bracknell, if you think it would be of any benefit in this discussion.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I really must insist that you stop questioning him, Mother. It's all perfectly irrelevant to our engagement, after all.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: For goodness' sake, Mother, can we please just leave now? I'm starting to feel like I'm being treated like a potential marriage prospect, rather than the daughter of a respectable lady.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid, Lady Bracknell, that my scars may not be of great relevance to the matter at hand, but I'm happy to show them to you if it would make you feel more at ease.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't wish to cause any further inconvenience, Lady Bracknell, but if you could perhaps tell me what specific information you're seeking, I'd be happy to try and provide it.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I'm telling you, Mother, this is ridiculous. I'm perfectly aware of Jack's background, and I assure you, I'm not some naive little girl who needs to be protected from the facts.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I refuse to have my own character and relationship with Jack questioned like this, Mother. Can't you see that it's humiliating?

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, I'm afraid you're being far too intrusive, and it's making me uncomfortable.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, that I am not one to shy away from the truth, and I am more than willing to provide any information you require, no matter how personal or potentially...embarrassing it may be.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
